title: Why Ownership Matters: Social Equity Licensing | The Bridge
description: A name on a package isn't a name on the paperwork. How New York defines equity ownership, and why a license is only the start.
lede: A name on a package and a name on the paperwork are two different things. One gets you a check. The other gets you the decisions.
html:
When High Times covered the launch of The Bridge, it drew the line that matters: Havoc isn't lending his name to a strain, he's an owner investing in the borough that raised him. That distinction is worth slowing down on, because this whole industry runs on it, and New York wrote it into law.

What ownership buys

A brand deal buys a logo. Ownership buys the decisions: who gets hired, whose products get shelf space, whose events fill the room, and where the money goes when the quarter closes. Those are the levers that decide whether what gets earned in a neighborhood has any reason to stay there.

Hold that up against the history. The state's own arrest mapping found that approximately one quarter of New Yorkers experienced three quarters of the arrests over four decades. If legal money then flows to owners with no tie to those blocks, all prohibition's end has done is change who benefits. The state says as much, calling it a key mandate that those harmed get an equitable chance to participate and thrive.

How New York defines it

To qualify for Social and Economic Equity status, sole control of the applicant has to rest with someone from an eligible group: a community disproportionately impacted, a minority-owned or women-owned business, distressed farmers or service-disabled veterans. For minority-owned and women-owned businesses, the law's definition asks for at least 51% ownership that is "real, substantial and continuing," with the authority to control day-to-day business decisions independently.

Read that phrasing and you can see what it's guarding against: a name on a form, with somebody else running the store. Extra priority goes to applicants who meet all of three tests. They are from an impacted community, they earn under 80% of their county's median income, and they have a cannabis conviction from before the law, or a close family member who does.

The state also looks behind the license. Applicants have to disclose true parties of interest, the people and entities with a stake in the business, and certain of them have to go through fingerprint-based background checks. A two-tier structure keeps anyone with an interest in growing, processing or distribution from holding an interest in retail, a design the state says is meant to prevent conflicts of interest, undue influence and market concentration.

Why a license isn't the finish line

The state reports that 56% of licenses are now held by equity applicants, past its 50% goal. It's a real number. But a license is a permission slip, not a business. It doesn't come with a storefront, or with operating money.

New York's own record shows the strain. The funding for its grant program for first-round retail licensees has been fully exhausted, and the state's site now points applicants and licensees to training hubs and support resources. The original law called for an incubator program offering counseling, small business coaching, financial planning and compliance help, which tells you the people who wrote it understood that qualifying was only the start. How many of those licenses turn into lasting businesses is a question the headline number can't answer.

What this has to do with your block

Nobody's asking you to buy something you don't want because of who owns the building. But you're allowed to ask. Every licensed shop is on the state's list. Ask who owns it, and check the answer against what they actually do.

Ours is on the About page: a partnership between Havoc of Mobb Deep and NDICA, a nonprofit working to lower barriers and open pathways for the communities most impacted by the War on Drugs. The stated goal goes past opening doors, to changing who gets to walk through them. Judge us on that. Come tell us how we're doing.
